title: Talking about the past and identifying people

grammarPoints.title: Past short forms
grammarPoints.meaning: Describe completed events and past states in plain form. These forms also fit inside quoted thoughts and other larger structures.
grammarPoints.formation: Verbs: change te-form て/で to た/だ. I-adjectives: い → かった. Nouns and na-adjectives: add だった. In any negative short form, change final ない to なかった.
notes: The irregular te-form of 行く gives 行った. する → した; 来る → 来た（きた）.
いい uses よかった and よくなかった. Do not put だった after an i-adjective.

grammarPoints.title: Casual questions and replies about the past
grammarPoints.meaning: Use past short forms when chatting with close friends or family. A rising tone makes a casual question.
grammarPoints.formation: Past short predicate + question intonation; do not add polite か. Keep だった in noun and na-adjective past questions and replies.
notes: Use うん/ううん in casual replies when appropriate. A reply can omit information already shared.
Changing the register does not change the time or polarity of the event.

grammarPoints.title: Thoughts about past events: とおもいます
grammarPoints.meaning: Give your current opinion or belief about a past event or state.
grammarPoints.formation: Past short clause + と思います. Put a negative belief inside the quoted clause: 〜なかったと思います.
notes: The event can be past while 思います remains nonpast: you think this now.
Do not use ました or でした before と in this pattern.

grammarPoints.title: Reporting statements about the past
grammarPoints.meaning: Report what another person said using a short-form quotation.
grammarPoints.formation: Speaker は + short clause + と言っていました. Preserve the time intended in the original statement.
notes: Japanese does not automatically shift a quoted nonpast form to past just because the reporting verb is past.
Context must distinguish “said they had done it” from “said they were doing it then.”

grammarPoints.title: Describing a noun with a clause
grammarPoints.meaning: Identify a person or thing by putting its description directly before the noun.
grammarPoints.formation: I-adjective + noun; na-adjective + な + noun; short verb clause + noun. For a visible ongoing action, use ている + 人.
notes: No relative pronoun equivalent to “who” is needed, and no の belongs between a verb and the noun.
This lesson concentrates on current actions and states; keep complex relative-clause constructions for later study.

grammarPoints.title: Already done and not done yet
grammarPoints.meaning: Distinguish a completed task with a present result from a task that is still pending.
grammarPoints.formation: もう + verb polite past; まだ + verb te-form + いません.
notes: For “not yet,” do not use the simple past negative: that describes a finished past period instead.
Use a context where completing the action matters now. Casual equivalents are もう〜た and まだ〜ていない.

grammarPoints.title: Reason first with から
grammarPoints.meaning: Join a reason and its consequence in one sentence.
grammarPoints.formation: Reason clause + から、result clause. A short noun or na-adjective affirmative reason keeps だ before から.
notes: A polite result can follow a short or polite reason. Use a short reason when the whole sentence is casual.
Choose causally compatible clauses; two unrelated facts do not make a useful explanation.

grammarPoints.title: Extra: color words before nouns
grammarPoints.meaning: Describe an object with either a color adjective or a color noun.
grammarPoints.formation: I-adjective color + noun; noun color + の + noun.
notes: 赤い and 白い are adjectives; 緑 and 紫 take の here. Do not automatically add い to every color.
Color nouns can also stand alone as the topic of a sentence.
